explanations.answer: The food offerings to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Moses says the priests "…are to eat the food offerings to the LORD; that is their inheritance." (Deuteronomy 18:1) The whole tribe of Levi has no portion or inheritance with Israel, so those offerings are what Moses names as theirs. That's a different kind of inheritance than the rest of Israel gets.

Manna is a real thing, friend. God told Moses He would rain down bread from heaven for Israel (Exodus 16:4). But that's not what Moses names here. He says the Levites eat the food offerings to the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:1).

I get why you'd pick it, baker, because spoils sound like a big payday. But Moses never mentions battle spoils for the Levites here. He says they "…are to eat the food offerings to the LORD; that is their inheritance." (Deuteronomy 18:1)

Yes, baker! Moses says, "…the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them." (Deuteronomy 18:2) The Levites have no inheritance among their brothers, but they have Him. And Moses says He is the One who promised it. The LORD Himself is what they get.

Nice guess, friend, but the law isn't the word Moses uses. He says the Levites have no inheritance among their brothers, "…the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them." (Deuteronomy 18:2) Their inheritance is a Person, not a rulebook.

A kingdom sounds like a big prize, baker. But that's not what Moses says. The Levites have no inheritance among their brothers, and then he says, "…the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them." (Deuteronomy 18:2)

That's right, baker. Moses says, "…the LORD your God has chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time." (Deuteronomy 18:5) So the gifts go with the job: standing and ministering in His name. And "…for all time." is no short-term contract.

Close in feeling, friend, but that's not the word in the verse. Moses says the LORD has "…chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time." (Deuteronomy 18:5) Levi was picked out of all the tribes for a job: to stand and minister in His name. The verse points to the choosing and the service.

Whoa, friend, exiled would be a plot twist! But that's not what Moses says. He says the LORD has "…chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time." (Deuteronomy 18:5) They're picked to serve, not sent away.

That's right, baker. Moses says the Levite "…shall eat equal portions, even though he has received money from the sale of his father’s estate." (Deuteronomy 18:8) So his side money doesn't shrink his share. Everybody at that table gets the same portion.

Not quite, friend. Moses says the Levite "…shall eat equal portions, even though he has received money from the sale of his father’s estate." (Deuteronomy 18:8) So the statement is true, and the portions stay equal even with that money in his pocket.

You got it, baker. Moses lists someone who "…consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead." (Deuteronomy 18:11) Those belong on the list of things Israel was not to do. It's a serious list, so we just keep it plain.

Nope, friend, that's not on Moses' list. The list in Deuteronomy 18:10-11 is about things like divination, sorcery, casting spells, consulting a medium or spiritist, and inquiring of the dead. Hiring a worker isn't in there.

That's a kind thing to do, baker, and it's not on the list at all. Moses names practices like casting spells, consulting "…a medium or spiritist…" and inquiring "…of the dead." (Deuteronomy 18:11) Welcoming a traveler isn't one of them.

Right on, baker. Moses says, "…because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you." (Deuteronomy 18:12) Just before that, he lists the things, like divination, sorcery and consulting a medium (Deuteronomy 18:10, 11). So the reason is the practices themselves, and Moses names them plainly.

explanations.answer: Because the nations were few in number
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend, but Moses doesn't say anything about how many people were in those nations. He says, "…because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you." (Deuteronomy 18:12) The reason is their practices.

explanations.answer: Because Israel had the bigger army
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, baker, since armies are the usual answer. But Moses gives a different reason. He says, "…because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you." (Deuteronomy 18:12)

Careful with this one, friend. Moses says the opposite: "…the LORD your God has not permitted you to do so." (Deuteronomy 18:14) The nations listen to conjurers and diviners, but Israel is told not to. So the statement is false.

That's right, baker. Moses says, "Though these nations, which you will dispossess, listen to conjurers and diviners, the LORD your God has not permitted you to do so." (Deuteronomy 18:14) The nations may do it, but Israel is not allowed to.

That's right, baker. Moses says, "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him." (Deuteronomy 18:15) This prophet comes from among their own brothers. The people already know where to look.
Not this time, friend. Moses says the prophet will come "…from among your brothers." (Deuteronomy 18:15) That means from among Israel itself, not from the nations around them.

Not this time, friend. Moses says the LORD "…will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers." (Deuteronomy 18:15) That means from among Israel's own people. Egypt's priests aren't mentioned anywhere in that sentence.

explanations.answer: Not to hear His voice anymore
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The people said, "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!" (Deuteronomy 18:16) I think that voice and that fire were more than they could stand. I bet my mustache would have stood straight up.

explanations.answer: To see His face up close
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite direction, friend. The people said, "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!" (Deuteronomy 18:16) They wanted less of it, not a closer look.

explanations.answer: To lead them back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, but that's not what they asked here. At Horeb, they said, "Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!" (Deuteronomy 18:16) Their request was about the voice and the fire. Going back to Egypt isn't in it.

I'm glad you checked, friend, because it's the other way around. The LORD said to Moses, "They have spoken well." (Deuteronomy 18:17) Moses doesn't say anything about anger. Then the LORD goes on to promise a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:18). So the statement is false.
That's right, baker. The LORD told Moses, "They have spoken well." (Deuteronomy 18:17) Moses doesn't say He was angry. Then the LORD goes on to promise a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:18).

That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him." (Deuteronomy 18:18) The prophet carries God's words, not his own. That's a pretty big job.

I see where that came from, friend, since fire was just in the story. But the LORD says, "I will put My words in his mouth…" (Deuteronomy 18:18) The word is words, and the prophet tells them everything God commands him.

Seals are my department, baker, since I seal cookie boxes! But that's not the word in this verse. The LORD says, "I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him." (Deuteronomy 18:18)

Right, baker. The LORD says, "…if any prophet dares to speak a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak, or to speak in the name of other gods, that prophet must be put to death." (Deuteronomy 18:20) It's a heavy verse, and I think it shows how seriously God takes His words. Two things are named here: speaking in His name what He didn't command, and speaking in the name of other gods.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "…if any prophet dares to speak a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak, or to speak in the name of other gods, that prophet must be put to death." (Deuteronomy 18:20) So the statement is true. It's a heavy verse, and we just read it as it is.

You got it, baker. Moses says, "When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken." (Deuteronomy 18:22) So a message that never comes true is one the LORD has not spoken. Then Moses adds that the prophet has spoken presumptuously, and tells the people, "Do not be afraid of him."

explanations.answer: It sounds too hard to obey
explanations.explanation: I get it, friend, hard words can feel suspicious. But Moses never gives that test. He says that if the message "…does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken." (Deuteronomy 18:22)

explanations.answer: The prophet is from another tribe
explanations.explanation: Interesting thought, baker, but Moses doesn't say a word about tribes here. He says that when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message "…does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken." (Deuteronomy 18:22) The question is what happens to the message. Where the prophet comes from never enters into it.
Careful, friend, Moses says the opposite. He says the prophet "…has spoken presumptuously. Do not be afraid of him." (Deuteronomy 18:22) So the statement is false.

That's right, baker. When the message doesn't come true, Moses says, "The prophet has spoken presumptuously. Do not be afraid of him." (Deuteronomy 18:22) No fear needed. I wish somebody had told that to me about the vacuum cleaner.
